examples: I clean my room every weekend.
I clean in the living room and rest.
I feel good because cleaning is done.
nuance: 청소 means cleaning a space such as a room or floor, and it almost always pairs with the verb 하다 in daily speech.
mistakes: Say 청소를 해요, not 청소가 해요, for the action.

usage: There is a lot of laundry.
examples: Today I want to do laundry.
I am busy because there is much laundry.
I hung the laundry in the morning.
nuance: 빨래 means both the washing of clothes and the laundry items themselves, and it commonly pairs with the verb 하다.
mistakes: Use 빨래를 해요, not 빨래를 만들어요, for doing wash.

usage: I wash dishes in the kitchen.
examples: After dinner I wash the dishes.
I do dishes in the kitchen and rest.
It is hard because there are many dishes.
nuance: 설거지 means washing used dishes after a meal, and it pairs with the verb 하다 rather than the verb 씻다 for the body.
mistakes: Say 설거지를 해요, not 설거지를 씻어요, for dishes.

examples: On the weekend I want to cook Korean food.
Cooking is hard so I do it slowly.
nuance: 요리 means both the act of cooking and the finished dish, and as an action it pairs with the verb 하다.
mistakes: Use 요리를 해요, not 요리를 먹어요, for the act.

usage: There is a lot of trash.
examples: Every evening I take out the trash.
It smells because there is much trash.
I separate the trash and throw it out.
nuance: 쓰레기 means garbage or waste, and unlike most chore words it usually pairs with the verb 버리다 to throw away.
mistakes: Say 쓰레기를 버려요, not 쓰레기를 해요, for trash.

examples: I tidy the top of the desk.
I organize clothes in the room and rest.
The room is clean because tidying is done.
nuance: 정리 means arranging or putting things in order, and as a chore it pairs with the verb 하다 in everyday talk.
mistakes: Use 정리를 해요, not 정리를 만들어요, for tidying.

examples: I take a shower every morning.
After exercise I shower in the bathroom.
I feel good because the shower is cool.
nuance: 샤워 means a stand up shower with running water, and it pairs with the verb 하다 rather than 씻다 for the whole body.
mistakes: Say 샤워를 해요, not 샤워를 먹어요, for showering.

usage: I wash my face in the bathroom.
examples: I wash my face right after waking.
In the morning I wash up in the bathroom.
I wash my face and brush my teeth.
nuance: 세수 means washing only the face and hands, so washing the whole body would use 샤워 or 목욕 instead in Korean.
mistakes: Use 세수를 해요 for the face, not the body.

usage: I brush my teeth in the bathroom.
examples: After eating I brush my teeth.
Before sleeping I brush in the bathroom.
I brush my teeth and drink water.
nuance: 양치 means brushing the teeth and is short for 양치질, and the full action pairs with the verb 하다.
mistakes: Say 양치를 해요, not 양치를 먹어요, for teeth.

examples: In the evening I want to take a walk.
I walk with my dog in the park.
I go out daily because walks are nice.
nuance: 산책 means a relaxed walk for pleasure, while walking somewhere as transport is usually said with the verb 걷다 instead.
mistakes: Use 산책을 해요, not 산책을 가요, for the act.

examples: On the weekend I want to rest fully.
After work I rest at home.
I slept early because I needed rest.
nuance: 휴식 is a slightly formal noun for taking a break, and in casual speech people often use the plain verb 쉬다 instead.
mistakes: 휴식 is a noun, so add 하다 for the action.

usage: I wash up before going out.
examples: I want to go out briefly in the afternoon.
I go out and come back in the evening.
Going out is hard because it rains.
nuance: 외출 means leaving home for a short trip outside, and it pairs with the verb 하다 in everyday speech.
mistakes: Use 외출을 해요, not 외출을 가요, for going out.
